# Solutions: Part IV {#sec-solutions-part-4}

Solutions to the exercises in Part IV, grouped by chapter, followed by the solutions to the Part IV review. Try each exercise before reading its solution. The link after each solution takes you back to its exercise.

## Eigenvalues and eigenvectors {#sec-solutions-eigenvalues}

Exercises from @sec-eigenvalues.

[**1.**]{#solution-eigenvalues-1} The trace is 7 and the determinant is $10 - 4 = 6$, so $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6 = 0$, giving $\lambda = 6$ or $1$. For $\lambda = 6$, $\M{A} - 6\M{I} = \mat{-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4}$; its first row says $-x + 2y = 0$, so $x = 2y$ and $\vect{v} = (2, 1)\T$ (the second row says the same thing, as it must). For $\lambda = 1$, $\M{A} - \M{I} = \mat{4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1}$, whose second row says $2x + y = 0$, so $\vect{v} = (1, -2)\T$. Check: $6 + 1 = 7$ is the trace and $6 \times 1 = 6$ is the determinant. ✓

[Back to exercise 1](../part-4/18-eigenvalues.qmd#exercise-eigenvalues-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-eigenvalues-2} The matrix is triangular, so the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: 2, $-1$ and 3. For $\lambda = 2$, the first column of $\M{A} - 2\M{I}$ is zero, so $\vect{v} = (1, 0, 0)\T$ works: $\M{A}\vect{v}$ is the first column of $\M{A}$, which is $(2, 0, 0)\T = 2\vect{v}$.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-4/18-eigenvalues.qmd#exercise-eigenvalues-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-eigenvalues-3} The matrix splits into a $2 \times 2$ block $\mat{1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1}$, with trace 2 and determinant $-3$, so eigenvalues 3 and $-1$, and the single entry 3. So the eigenvalues are 3 (twice) and $-1$.

For $\lambda = 3$, $\M{A} - 3\M{I} = \mat{-2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0}$, which says only $x = y$, so the eigenspace is the plane spanned by $(1, 1, 0)\T$ and $(0, 0, 1)\T$, of dimension 2. For $\lambda = -1$, the eigenspace is the line through $(1, -1, 0)\T$. The repeated eigenvalue has two independent eigenvectors, so the matrix is not defective.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-4/18-eigenvalues.qmd#exercise-eigenvalues-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-eigenvalues-4} (a) $(\M{A} + c\M{I})\vect{v} = \M{A}\vect{v} + c\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v} + c\vect{v} = (\lambda + c)\vect{v}$.\
(b) Multiply $\M{A}\vect{v} = \lambda\vect{v}$ on the left by $\M{A}^{-1}$: $\vect{v} = \lambda\M{A}^{-1}\vect{v}$. Since $\M{A}$ is invertible, $\lambda \neq 0$ (otherwise $\M{A}\vect{v} = \zerovec$ with $\vect{v} \neq \zerovec$), so dividing by $\lambda$ gives $\M{A}^{-1}\vect{v} = \tfrac{1}{\lambda}\vect{v}$.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-4/18-eigenvalues.qmd#exercise-eigenvalues-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-eigenvalues-5} The trace is 0 and the determinant is 4, so $\lambda^2 + 4 = 0$ and $\lambda = \pm 2i$. The matrix is $2\mat{0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0}$: a rotation by $90°$ followed by scaling by 2. No direction is left on its own line, which is why there are no real eigenvalues.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-4/18-eigenvalues.qmd#exercise-eigenvalues-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-eigenvalues-6} The discriminant of $\lambda^2 - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc) = 0$ is
$$
(a + d)^2 - 4(ad - bc) = (a - d)^2 + 4bc.
$$
If $b$ and $c$ have the same sign, $bc > 0$, so the discriminant is positive and both eigenvalues are real (and different).

[Back to exercise 6](../part-4/18-eigenvalues.qmd#exercise-eigenvalues-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-eigenvalues-7}

The eigenvalues are $2 - \sqrt{2} \approx 0.586$, $2$ and $2 + \sqrt{2} \approx 3.414$, with eigenvectors proportional to $(1, \sqrt{2}, 1)$, $(-1, 0, 1)$ and $(1, -\sqrt{2}, 1)$ (software may flip their signs).

- Lowest frequency: all three masses move the same way together, the middle one furthest.
- Middle frequency: the outer masses move in opposite directions and the middle one stays still.
- Highest frequency: the outer masses move together and the middle one moves the opposite way, by more.

The more the neighbouring masses move against each other, the more the springs between them stretch, and the higher the frequency.

## Diagonalisation and matrix powers {#sec-solutions-diagonalisation}

Exercises from @sec-diagonalisation.

[**1.**]{#solution-diagonalisation-1} The trace is 2 and the determinant $-3$, so $\lambda = 3$ or $-1$, with eigenvectors $(1, 1)\T$ and $(1, -1)\T$. So
$$
\M{P} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1},
\qquad
\M{D} = \mat{3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1},
\qquad
\M{P}^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1}.
$$
Then $\M{D}^{10} = \mat{3^{10} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{10}} = \mat{59049 & 0 \\ 0 & 1}$, and $\M{P}\M{D}^{10} = \mat{3^{10} & 1 \\ 3^{10} & -1}$ (each column of $\M{P}$ scaled by its eigenvalue to the 10th power), so
$$
\M{A}^{10} = \M{P}\M{D}^{10}\M{P}^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\mat{3^{10} + 1 & 3^{10} - 1 \\ 3^{10} - 1 & 3^{10} + 1} = \mat{29525 & 29524 \\ 29524 & 29525}.
$$

[Back to exercise 1](../part-4/19-diagonalisation.qmd#exercise-diagonalisation-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-diagonalisation-2} With $\vect{x}_k$ holding the shares of brands 1 and 2, each column of $\M{M}$ says where one brand's customers go:
$$
\M{M} = \mat{0.7 & 0.4 \\ 0.3 & 0.6}.
$$
The columns add to 1, so 1 is an eigenvalue, and the other is the trace minus 1, which is $0.3$. For $\lambda = 1$, $\M{M} - \M{I} = \mat{-0.3 & 0.4 \\ 0.3 & -0.4}$, giving the eigenvector $(4, 3)\T$. Scaled to add to 1, the long-run shares are $\tfrac{4}{7} \approx 57\%$ for brand 1 and $\tfrac{3}{7} \approx 43\%$ for brand 2. The distance from the steady state is multiplied by $0.3$ each month, so it is approached quickly: after 4 months, less than 1% of the starting difference is left.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-4/19-diagonalisation.qmd#exercise-diagonalisation-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-diagonalisation-3} The only eigenvalue is 2 (twice), and $\M{A} - 2\M{I} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0}$ has rank 1, so its null space, the eigenspace, is the line through $(1, 0)\T$. There aren't two independent eigenvectors to make an invertible $\M{P}$, so the matrix can't be diagonalised.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-4/19-diagonalisation.qmd#exercise-diagonalisation-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-diagonalisation-4} Using $\det(\M{X}\M{Y}) = \det\M{X}\det\M{Y}$ and $\det\M{P}^{-1} = 1/\det\M{P}$ (@sec-determinants),
$$
\det\M{A} = \det\M{P}\,\det\M{D}\,\det\M{P}^{-1} = \det\M{D} = \lambda_1\lambda_2\cdots\lambda_n,
$$
since the determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-4/19-diagonalisation.qmd#exercise-diagonalisation-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-diagonalisation-5} As in Example 3, the vector $(L_{k+1}, L_k)\T$ is multiplied by $\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0}$ at each step, so by @eq-modes it is a combination of $\lambda_1^k$ and $\lambda_2^k$ times the eigenvectors. Its second entry is therefore $L_k = a\lambda_1^k + b\lambda_2^k$ for some numbers $a$ and $b$. The starting values give
$$
a + b = L_0 = 2,
\qquad
a\lambda_1 + b\lambda_2 = L_1 = 1.
$$
Since $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 1$ (the trace), $a = b = 1$ satisfies both, and the two equations have only one solution because $\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2$. So $L_k = \lambda_1^k + \lambda_2^k$.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-4/19-diagonalisation.qmd#exercise-diagonalisation-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-diagonalisation-6} $\M{A} = \M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1}$ with $\M{D} = \mat{1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1}$, so $\M{A}^2 = \M{P}\M{D}^2\M{P}^{-1} = \M{P}\M{I}\M{P}^{-1} = \M{I}$. A reflection in a line is an example: vectors along the mirror line have eigenvalue 1, vectors perpendicular to it have eigenvalue $-1$, and reflecting twice puts everything back.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-4/19-diagonalisation.qmd#exercise-diagonalisation-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-diagonalisation-7}

## Symmetric matrices and quadratic forms {#sec-solutions-symmetric-matrices}

Exercises from @sec-symmetric-matrices.

[**1.**]{#solution-symmetric-matrices-1} The trace is 0 and the determinant $-25$, so $\lambda = \pm 5$. For $\lambda = 5$, $\M{A} - 5\M{I} = \mat{-2 & 4 \\ 4 & -8}$, giving $(2, 1)\T$; for $\lambda = -5$, the eigenvector is $(1, -2)\T$, perpendicular to the first. Normalising,
$$
\M{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2},
\qquad
\M{\Lambda} = \mat{5 & 0 \\ 0 & -5}.
$$

[Back to exercise 1](../part-4/20-symmetric-matrices.qmd#exercise-symmetric-matrices-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-symmetric-matrices-2}

Split each cross term equally between the two off-diagonal entries. For a $2 \times 2$ matrix the eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2 - (\text{trace})\lambda + \det = 0$.

(a) The matrix is $\mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2}$, with trace 4 and determinant 3, so $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 = 0$ and the eigenvalues are 3 and 1: positive definite.

(b) The matrix is $\mat{1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1}$, with trace 2 and determinant $-8$, so $\lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 8 = (\lambda - 4)(\lambda + 2) = 0$ and the eigenvalues are 4 and $-2$: indefinite. For example, $(1, -1)$ gives $1 - 6 + 1 = -4$.

(c) The matrix is $\mat{1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4}$, with trace 5 and determinant 0, so the eigenvalues are 5 and 0: positive semidefinite. In fact $x^2 - 4xy + 4y^2 = (x - 2y)^2$, which is zero along the line $x = 2y$.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-4/20-symmetric-matrices.qmd#exercise-symmetric-matrices-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-symmetric-matrices-3} A symmetric $2 \times 2$ matrix is positive definite when its top-left entry and its determinant are both positive. Here $2 > 0$, and $16 - k^2 > 0$ when $-4 < k < 4$.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-4/20-symmetric-matrices.qmd#exercise-symmetric-matrices-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-symmetric-matrices-4} $\ell_{11} = \sqrt{4} = 2$, then $\ell_{21} = 2/2 = 1$, then $\ell_{22} = \sqrt{10 - 1^2} = 3$:
$$
\M{L} = \mat{2 & 0 \\ 1 & 3},
\qquad
\M{L}\M{L}\T = \mat{4 & 2 \\ 2 & 10}. \;✓
$$

[Back to exercise 4](../part-4/20-symmetric-matrices.qmd#exercise-symmetric-matrices-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-symmetric-matrices-5} $(\M{A}\T\M{A})\T = \M{A}\T(\M{A}\T)\T = \M{A}\T\M{A}$, so it is symmetric. For any $\vect{x}$,
$$
\vect{x}\T\M{A}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = (\M{A}\vect{x})\T(\M{A}\vect{x}) = \lVert\M{A}\vect{x}\rVert^2 \ge 0,
$$
so it is positive semidefinite. This is zero only when $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$. If the columns of $\M{A}$ are independent, that happens only for $\vect{x} = \zerovec$, so the matrix is positive definite.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-4/20-symmetric-matrices.qmd#exercise-symmetric-matrices-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-symmetric-matrices-6} The characteristic equation is $\lambda^2 - (a + c)\lambda + (ac - b^2) = 0$, with discriminant
$$
(a + c)^2 - 4(ac - b^2) = a^2 - 2ac + c^2 + 4b^2 = (a - c)^2 + 4b^2 \ge 0,
$$
so the eigenvalues are real. They are equal only when $a = c$ and $b = 0$, when the matrix is a multiple of $\M{I}$.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-4/20-symmetric-matrices.qmd#exercise-symmetric-matrices-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-symmetric-matrices-7}

## The singular value decomposition and PCA {#sec-solutions-svd-pca}

Exercises from @sec-svd-pca.

[**1.**]{#solution-svd-pca-1} $\M{A}\T\M{A} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}$, with eigenvalues 2 and 0, so the singular values are $\sqrt{2}$ and 0. The matrix sends $(x, y)$ to $(x + y, 0)$: it flattens the unit circle onto the segment of the $x$ axis from $-\sqrt{2}$ to $\sqrt{2}$, reached from the direction $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)$. The zero singular value shows the rank is 1.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-4/21-svd-pca.qmd#exercise-svd-pca-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-svd-pca-2} The matrix stretches by 2 along $x$ and by 3 along $y$ (with a flip), so $\sigma_1 = 3$ and $\sigma_2 = 2$, in decreasing order. Take $\vect{v}_1 = (0, 1)\T$; then $\vect{u}_1 = \M{A}\vect{v}_1/3 = (0, -1)\T$. Take $\vect{v}_2 = (1, 0)\T$; then $\vect{u}_2 = \M{A}\vect{v}_2/2 = (1, 0)\T$. So
$$
\mat{2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0}\mat{3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2}\mat{0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0}.
$$
The minus sign belongs in $\M{U}$, because singular values are never negative.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-4/21-svd-pca.qmd#exercise-svd-pca-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-svd-pca-3} Transposing $\M{A} = \M{U}\M{\Sigma}\M{V}\T$ gives $\M{A}\T = \M{V}\M{\Sigma}\T\M{U}\T$. This is an SVD of $\M{A}\T$: $\M{V}$ and $\M{U}$ are orthogonal, and $\M{\Sigma}\T$ has the same singular values down its diagonal.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-4/21-svd-pca.qmd#exercise-svd-pca-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-svd-pca-4} The original needs $500 \times 800 = 400\,000$ numbers. The rank-40 approximation needs $40(500 + 800 + 1) = 52\,040$, which is about 13% of the original.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-4/21-svd-pca.qmd#exercise-svd-pca-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-svd-pca-5} An orthogonal matrix $\M{Q}$ has determinant $\pm 1$, since $(\det\M{Q})^2 = \det(\M{Q}\T\M{Q}) = \det\M{I} = 1$. So
$$
\lvert\det\M{A}\rvert = \lvert\det\M{U}\rvert\,\lvert\det\M{\Sigma}\rvert\,\lvert\det\M{V}\T\rvert = \det\M{\Sigma} = \sigma_1\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_n.
$$

[Back to exercise 5](../part-4/21-svd-pca.qmd#exercise-svd-pca-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-svd-pca-6} $\M{A}\T\M{A} = \mat{2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2}$ has eigenvalues 4 and 0, so $\sigma_1 = 2$, with $\vect{v}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)\T$ and $\vect{u}_1 = \M{A}\vect{v}_1/2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)\T$. Only the non-zero singular value is inverted, so
$$
\M{A}^+ = \frac{1}{\sigma_1}\vect{v}_1\vect{u}_1\T = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1} = \frac{1}{4}\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}.
$$
Then $\hat{\vect{x}} = \M{A}^+(1, 3)\T = (1, 1)\T$. Every vector with $x_1 + x_2 = 2$ is a least-squares solution (each gives $\M{A}\vect{x} = (2, 2)\T$, the projection of $\vect{b}$), and $(1, 1)$ is the one closest to the origin.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-4/21-svd-pca.qmd#exercise-svd-pca-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-svd-pca-7}

::: {#2cfd7e44 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
h = rng.normal(170, 10, 200)               # heights in cm
s = h + rng.normal(0, 4, 200)              # arm spans in cm
X = np.column_stack([h, s])
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
U, sv, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
print(Vt)                                  # rows are the principal components
print(sv**2 / np.sum(sv**2))               # fraction of variance explained
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
[[-0.67484712 -0.73795756]
 [ 0.73795756 -0.67484712]]
[0.96746956 0.03253044]
```
:::
:::


In MATLAB, the same steps are `X = [h, s]; Xc = X - mean(X); [~, S, V] = svd(Xc, 'econ'); diag(S).^2 / sum(diag(S).^2)`. MATLAB's random numbers differ from NumPy's, so the results differ slightly.

The first principal component is about $\pm(0.67, 0.74)$ and explains about 97% of the variance: it is overall body size, with height and arm span increasing together. The second, perpendicular to it, explains the remaining 3%; it measures how much longer or shorter a person's arm span is than you would expect from their height. One number per person, the score along the first component, captures almost all the information in the two measurements.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-4/21-svd-pca.qmd#exercise-svd-pca-7){.sol-link}

## Derivatives with vectors and matrices {#sec-solutions-matrix-calculus}

Exercises from @sec-matrix-calculus.

[**1.**]{#solution-matrix-calculus-1} $f = \vect{a}\T\vect{x}$ with $\vect{a} = (3, -2, 1)\T$, so $\nabla f = (3, -2, 1)\T$. Expanding, $g = \vect{x}\T\vect{x} - 2\vect{c}\T\vect{x} + \vect{c}\T\vect{c}$, so $\nabla g = 2\vect{x} - 2\vect{c} = 2(\vect{x} - \vect{c})$, pointing directly away from $\vect{c}$.

[Back to exercise 1](../part-4/22-matrix-calculus.qmd#exercise-matrix-calculus-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-matrix-calculus-2} $\M{A} + \M{A}\T = \mat{2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6}$, so the gradient is $(2x_1 + 2x_2, \; 2x_1 + 6x_2)\T$. Written out, $\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = x_1^2 + 2x_1x_2 + 3x_2^2$, whose partial derivatives are $2x_1 + 2x_2$ and $2x_1 + 6x_2$. ✓

[Back to exercise 2](../part-4/22-matrix-calculus.qmd#exercise-matrix-calculus-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-matrix-calculus-3} Row $i$ of the Jacobian holds the partial derivatives of $f_i$. For $f_1 = x^2y$, $\partial f_1/\partial x = 2xy$ (treating $y$ as a constant) and $\partial f_1/\partial y = x^2$. For $f_2 = x + \sin y$, $\partial f_2/\partial x = 1$ and $\partial f_2/\partial y = \cos y$. So
$$
\M{J} = \mat{\partial f_1/\partial x & \partial f_1/\partial y \\ \partial f_2/\partial x & \partial f_2/\partial y} = \mat{2xy & x^2 \\ 1 & \cos y},
\qquad
\M{J}(1, 0) = \mat{0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}.
$$

[Back to exercise 3](../part-4/22-matrix-calculus.qmd#exercise-matrix-calculus-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-matrix-calculus-4} $\nabla f = (2x + y - 3, \; x + 2y)\T = \zerovec$ gives $x = -2y$, then $-4y + y = 3$, so $y = -1$ and $x = 2$. The Hessian is $\mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2}$ at every point, with eigenvalues 3 and 1, so $(2, -1)$ is a minimum, where $f = 4 - 2 + 1 - 6 = -3$. Since the Hessian is positive definite everywhere, it is the global minimum.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-4/22-matrix-calculus.qmd#exercise-matrix-calculus-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-matrix-calculus-5} With $(x, y) = \vect{g}(u, v) = (u + v, \; uv)$,
$$
\M{J}_{\vect{g}} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ v & u},
\qquad
\M{J}_f = \mat{2x & -1} = \mat{2(u + v) & -1},
$$
so
$$
\M{J}_h = \M{J}_f\M{J}_{\vect{g}} = \mat{2(u + v) - v & 2(u + v) - u} = \mat{2u + v & u + 2v}.
$$
Substituting first, $h = (u + v)^2 - uv = u^2 + uv + v^2$, whose partial derivatives are $2u + v$ and $u + 2v$. ✓

[Back to exercise 5](../part-4/22-matrix-calculus.qmd#exercise-matrix-calculus-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-matrix-calculus-6} The first term has gradient $2\M{A}\T\M{A}\vect{x} - 2\M{A}\T\vect{b}$ (as in the chapter), and $\mu\vect{x}\T\vect{x}$ has gradient $2\mu\vect{x}$. Setting the sum to zero gives $(\M{A}\T\M{A} + \mu\M{I})\vect{x} = \M{A}\T\vect{b}$. For any $\vect{x} \neq \zerovec$,
$$
\vect{x}\T(\M{A}\T\M{A} + \mu\M{I})\vect{x} = \lVert\M{A}\vect{x}\rVert^2 + \mu\lVert\vect{x}\rVert^2 > 0,
$$
so the matrix is positive definite, hence invertible, whatever the columns of $\M{A}$. Adding $\mu\M{I}$ raises every eigenvalue of $\M{A}\T\M{A}$ by $\mu$, lifting the zero ones away from zero.

```{.text .code-output}
alpha = 0.21: 1000 steps, |x| = 2.47e+41
```
:::

The eigenvalues of $\M{A}$ are 10 and 1, and each step multiplies the two components of $\vect{x}$ by $1 - 10\alpha$ and $1 - \alpha$.

- $\alpha = 0.1$: the factors are 0 and $0.9$. The first component vanishes at once, but the second shrinks slowly, and $0.9^k < 10^{-6}$ needs $k = 132$.
- $\alpha = 0.18$: the factors are $-0.8$ and $0.82$, both well inside $(-1, 1)$, so about 70 steps. This is close to the best possible, $\alpha = 2/(10 + 1) \approx 0.182$, which makes both factors $\pm 9/11$.
- $\alpha = 0.21$: the factor $1 - 2.1 = -1.1$ has size greater than 1, so the first component flips sign and grows at every step, and the method diverges.

Convergence needs $\alpha < 2/\lambda_{\max} = 0.2$, and even the best step leaves a factor of $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$ per step, where $\kappa = 10$ is the condition number.

## Linear ODE systems and the matrix exponential {#sec-solutions-linear-odes}

Exercises from @sec-linear-odes.

[**1.**]{#solution-linear-odes-1} With $x_1 = x$, $x_2 = \dot{x}$: $\dot{x}_1 = x_2$ and $\dot{x}_2 = -2x_1 - 3x_2$, so $\M{A} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3}$. The trace is $-3$ and the determinant 2, so $\lambda^2 + 3\lambda + 2 = 0$ and $\lambda = -1, -2$. Both are real and negative: a stable node. The mass returns to rest without oscillating (it is overdamped).

[Back to exercise 1](../part-4/23-linear-odes.qmd#exercise-linear-odes-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-linear-odes-2} The eigenvalues are 3 and $-1$, with eigenvectors $(1, 1)\T$ and $(1, -1)\T$, and $(1, 0)\T = \tfrac{1}{2}(1, 1)\T + \tfrac{1}{2}(1, -1)\T$. So
$$
\vect{x}(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{3t}\mat{1 \\ 1} + \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-t}\mat{1 \\ -1}.
$$
The second mode dies away and the first grows, so $\vect{x}(t)$ grows without limit along the direction $(1, 1)$. The equilibrium is a saddle.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-4/23-linear-odes.qmd#exercise-linear-odes-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-linear-odes-3}

(a) $\tau = 0$, $\Delta = 4$: a centre, with $\lambda = \pm 2i$. This is the undamped spring $\ddot{x} + 4x = 0$.

(b) $\tau = 2$, $\Delta = -3 + 8 = 5$, and $\tau^2 - 4\Delta = -16 < 0$: an unstable spiral, with $\lambda = 1 \pm 2i$.

(c) $\tau = -6$, $\Delta = 8$, and $\tau^2 - 4\Delta = 4 > 0$: a stable node, with $\lambda = -2$ and $-4$.

(d) $\Delta = -2 < 0$: a saddle. The matrix is diagonal, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, $\lambda = 2$ and $-1$.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-4/23-linear-odes.qmd#exercise-linear-odes-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-linear-odes-4} (a) $\M{D}^k = \mat{a^k & 0 \\ 0 & b^k}$, so the series is
$$
\mat{1 + at + \tfrac{(at)^2}{2!} + \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & 1 + bt + \tfrac{(bt)^2}{2!} + \cdots} = \mat{e^{at} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{bt}}.
$$
(b) $\M{N}^2 = \M{0}$, so every term after $\M{N}t$ vanishes and $e^{\M{N}t} = \M{I} + \M{N}t = \mat{1 & t \\ 0 & 1}$. Then
$$
\vect{x}(t) = \mat{1 & t \\ 0 & 1}\mat{x_1(0) \\ x_2(0)} = \mat{x_1(0) + x_2(0)t \\ x_2(0)}.
$$
This is $\ddot{x} = 0$ written as a system: an object moving at constant velocity $x_2$, with no force on it. The factor $t$ is the polynomial growth that defective matrices bring.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-4/23-linear-odes.qmd#exercise-linear-odes-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-linear-odes-5} As a system, $\M{A} = \mat{0 & 1 \\ -4 & -c}$, with characteristic equation $\lambda^2 + c\lambda + 4 = 0$. The eigenvalues are complex, so the mass oscillates, when $c^2 - 16 < 0$, that is $0 \le c < 4$ (for $c = 0$ it oscillates for ever). At $c = 4$, $\lambda = -2$ is repeated: **critical damping**, where the mass returns to rest as fast as possible without overshooting. Car suspensions and door closers are designed to be close to this.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-4/23-linear-odes.qmd#exercise-linear-odes-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-linear-odes-6} Let $\vect{q}_1, \dots, \vect{q}_n$ be orthonormal eigenvectors, with eigenvalues $\lambda_i < 0$, and write $\vect{x}_0 = c_1\vect{q}_1 + \dots + c_n\vect{q}_n$. Then $\vect{x}(t) = \sum c_ie^{\lambda_i t}\vect{q}_i$, and because the $\vect{q}_i$ are orthonormal,
$$
\lVert\vect{x}(t)\rVert^2 = c_1^2e^{2\lambda_1 t} + \dots + c_n^2e^{2\lambda_n t}.
$$
Every term decreases and tends to 0 as $t$ grows, since every $\lambda_i < 0$. (For a matrix that is not symmetric, $\lVert\vect{x}\rVert$ can grow for a while before decaying, even when all the eigenvalues are negative.)

[Back to exercise 6](../part-4/23-linear-odes.qmd#exercise-linear-odes-6){.sol-link}

The matrix is triangular, so the eigenvalues are $-0.5$ and $-0.2$. Solving directly, $x_1 = 100e^{-0.5t}$, and
$$
x_2(t) = \frac{100 \times 0.5}{0.5 - 0.2}\left(e^{-0.2t} - e^{-0.5t}\right) = \frac{500}{3}\left(e^{-0.2t} - e^{-0.5t}\right).
$$
This is greatest when $\dot{x}_2 = 0$, that is $0.2e^{-0.2t} = 0.5e^{-0.5t}$, so $e^{0.3t} = 2.5$ and $t = \ln 2.5/0.3 \approx 3.05$ hours, when $x_2 \approx 54.3$ mg. The computed peak agrees, to the resolution of the time grid.

## Part IV review {#sec-solutions-review-4}

Exercises from the [Part IV review](../part-4/review.qmd).

[**1.**]{#solution-review-4-1} *Uses @sec-eigenvalues and @sec-diagonalisation.* $\det(\M{A} - \lambda\M{I}) = (2 - \lambda)^2 - 1 = 0$ gives $\lambda = 3$, with eigenvector $(1, 1)$, and $\lambda = 1$, with eigenvector $(1, -1)$. So $\M{A} = \M{V}\M{\Lambda}\M{V}^{-1}$ with $\M{V} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1}$ and $\M{V}^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1}$. Then $\M{V}\M{\Lambda}^{10} = \mat{3^{10} & 1 \\ 3^{10} & -1}$, and
$$
\M{A}^{10} = \M{V}\mat{3^{10} & 0 \\ 0 & 1}\M{V}^{-1}
= \frac{1}{2}\mat{3^{10} + 1 & 3^{10} - 1 \\ 3^{10} - 1 & 3^{10} + 1}
= \mat{29525 & 29524 \\ 29524 & 29525}.
$$

[Back to exercise 1](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-1){.sol-link}

[**2.**]{#solution-review-4-2} *Uses @sec-eigenvalues and @sec-diagonalisation.* With the state (town, suburbs), each column says where the people in one place go:
$$\M{T} = \mat{0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8}.$$
The trace is 1.7 and the determinant is 0.7, so the eigenvalues are 1 and 0.7. For $\lambda = 1$, $-0.1x_1 + 0.2x_2 = 0$, so $x_1 = 2x_2$: in the long run, $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the people live in the town and $\tfrac{1}{3}$ in the suburbs. The difference from this split is a multiple of the other eigenvector, which shrinks by a factor of 0.7 each year: it roughly halves every two years, and is under 1% of its starting size after 13 years.

[Back to exercise 2](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-2){.sol-link}

[**3.**]{#solution-review-4-3} *Uses @sec-symmetric-matrices.* The curve is $\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = 6$ with $\M{A} = \mat{5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2}$. Its trace is 7 and its determinant 6, so $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6 = (\lambda - 6)(\lambda - 1) = 0$. For $\lambda = 6$, $\M{A} - 6\M{I} = \mat{-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4}$ gives $x = 2y$, so the eigenvalues are 6, with unit eigenvector $(2, 1)/\sqrt{5}$, and 1, with the perpendicular unit eigenvector $(-1, 2)/\sqrt{5}$. In coordinates $u$, $v$ along these directions, the curve is $6u^2 + v^2 = 6$, or
$$u^2 + \frac{v^2}{6} = 1.$$
Both eigenvalues are positive, so it is an ellipse: half-length 1 along $(2, 1)$, and $\sqrt{6} \approx 2.45$ along $(-1, 2)$. From the matrix alone: $\det\M{A} = 6 > 0$ and the trace is positive, so both eigenvalues are positive. A negative determinant would mean eigenvalues of opposite signs, and a hyperbola.

[Back to exercise 3](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-3){.sol-link}

[**4.**]{#solution-review-4-4} *Uses @sec-svd-pca and @sec-floating-point-conditioning.*
$$\M{A}\T\M{A} = \mat{25 & 20 \\ 20 & 25},$$
with trace 50 and determinant $625 - 400 = 225$, so its eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2 - 50\lambda + 225 = (\lambda - 45)(\lambda - 5) = 0$. They are $45$ and $5$, so $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5} \approx 6.71$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$. Their product is $\sqrt{225} = 15 = \lvert\det\M{A}\rvert$. The condition number is $\kappa_2 = \sigma_1/\sigma_2 = 3$. The nearest singular matrix is found by setting $\sigma_2$ to zero, so its distance from $\M{A}$ is $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{5}$.

[Back to exercise 4](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-4){.sol-link}

[**5.**]{#solution-review-4-5} *Uses @sec-linear-odes and @sec-eigenvalues.* The trace is $-4$ and the determinant $4 - 1 = 3$, so $\lambda^2 + 4\lambda + 3 = (\lambda + 1)(\lambda + 3) = 0$. For $\lambda = -1$, $\M{A} + \M{I} = \mat{-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1}$ gives $x_1 = x_2$; for $\lambda = -3$, $\M{A} + 3\M{I} = \mat{1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}$ gives $x_1 = -x_2$. So the eigenvalues are $-1$, with eigenvector $(1, 1)$, and $-3$, with eigenvector $(1, -1)$. Writing $\vect{x}(0) = \tfrac{1}{2}(1, 1) + \tfrac{1}{2}(1, -1)$,
$$
\vect{x}(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-t}\mat{1 \\ 1} + \tfrac{1}{2}e^{-3t}\mat{1 \\ -1},
$$
that is, $x_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}(e^{-t} + e^{-3t})$ and $x_2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(e^{-t} - e^{-3t})$. The $(1, -1)$ part, the *difference* between the two temperatures, dies away fastest, at rate 3: the two objects quickly reach the same temperature. The $(1, 1)$ part, their shared temperature, then decays more slowly, at rate 1, as they both cool towards the surroundings.

[Back to exercise 5](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-5){.sol-link}

[**6.**]{#solution-review-4-6} *Uses @sec-matrix-calculus and @sec-symmetric-matrices.* For symmetric $\M{A}$, the gradient is $\nabla f = 2\M{A}\vect{x} - 2\vect{b}$. Setting it to zero gives $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$, that is $2x_1 + x_2 = 1$ and $x_1 + 2x_2 = 1$. Subtracting, $x_1 = x_2$, and then $3x_1 = 1$, so $\vect{x} = (\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{1}{3})$. There, $\vect{x}\T\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{x}\T\vect{b} = \tfrac{2}{3}$ and $2\vect{b}\T\vect{x} = \tfrac{4}{3}$, so
$$f = \tfrac{2}{3} - \tfrac{4}{3} = -\tfrac{2}{3}.$$
The Hessian is $2\M{A}$, and $\M{A}$ has eigenvalues 3 and 1 (exercise 1), both positive. So $\M{A}$ is positive definite, $f$ is a bowl, and this point is its minimum.

[Back to exercise 6](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-6){.sol-link}

[**7.**]{#solution-review-4-7} *Uses @sec-eigenvalues and @sec-linear-odes.* $\det(\M{B} - \lambda\M{I}) = (1 - \lambda)^2 + 2 = 0$ gives $\lambda = 1 \pm i\sqrt{2}$, with $\lvert\lambda\rvert = \sqrt{3}$. Complex eigenvalues mean rotation: the vectors $\M{B}^k\vect{x}_0$ turn round the origin and, since $\lvert\lambda\rvert > 1$, spiral outwards, growing by a factor of about $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ per step. The solutions of $d\vect{x}/dt = \M{B}\vect{x}$ also spiral outwards, because the real part 1 is positive: they grow like $e^t$ while rotating with angular frequency $\sqrt{2}$.

[Back to exercise 7](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-7){.sol-link}

[**8.**]{#solution-review-4-8} *Uses @sec-diagonalisation, @sec-determinants and @sec-inverses.* The two directions are eigenvectors: $(2, 1)\T$ with eigenvalue 4 and $(1, 1)\T$ with eigenvalue 1. So $\M{A} = \M{P}\M{D}\M{P}^{-1}$ with $\M{P} = \mat{2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1}$ and $\M{D} = \operatorname{diag}(4, 1)$. Here $\det\M{P} = 1$, so $\M{P}^{-1} = \mat{1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2}$, and
$$
\M{A} = \mat{8 & 1 \\ 4 & 1}\mat{1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2} = \mat{7 & -6 \\ 3 & -2}.
$$
Check: $\M{A}(2, 1)\T = (8, 4)\T = 4(2, 1)\T$ and $\M{A}(1, 1)\T = (1, 1)\T$. ✓ Then $\det\M{A} = -14 + 18 = 4$, the product of the eigenvalues: every area is multiplied by 4. The inverse is
$$
\M{A}^{-1} = \frac{1}{4}\mat{-2 & 6 \\ -3 & 7}.
$$
It has the same eigenvectors, with eigenvalues $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and 1: it shrinks $(2, 1)\T$ to a quarter of its length, and still leaves $(1, 1)\T$ unchanged.

[Back to exercise 8](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-8){.sol-link}

[**9.**]{#solution-review-4-9} *Uses @sec-gauss-jordan-rank, @sec-fundamental-subspaces, @sec-eigenvalues and @sec-symmetric-matrices.* Every entry of $\M{B} - \M{I}$ is 1, so its reduced row echelon form has one non-zero row, $(1, 1, 1)$: the rank is 1. So $\M{B} - \M{I}$ is singular and 1 is an eigenvalue, and by the rank–nullity theorem its eigenspace, the null space of $\M{B} - \M{I}$, has dimension $3 - 1 = 2$. It is the plane $x + y + z = 0$; setting each free variable to 1 in turn gives the basis $(-1, 1, 0)\T$ and $(-1, 0, 1)\T$.

The eigenvalues add up to the trace, 6, so the third is $6 - 1 - 1 = 4$. Indeed $\M{B}(1, 1, 1)\T = (4, 4, 4)\T$, so its eigenvector is $(1, 1, 1)\T$. Its dot products with the basis vectors are $-1 + 1 + 0 = 0$ and $-1 + 0 + 1 = 0$, so it is perpendicular to the whole eigenspace. This was bound to happen: $\M{B}$ is symmetric, and eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix for different eigenvalues are always perpendicular.

[Back to exercise 9](../part-4/review.qmd#exercise-review-4-9){.sol-link}

[**10.**]{#solution-review-4-10} *Uses @sec-transformations, @sec-basis-change, @sec-eigenvalues and @sec-diagonalisation.* A vector along the mirror, $(1, 2)\T$, is unchanged, so it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. A vector across it, $(-2, 1)\T$, is reversed, so it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $-1$. Check: $\M{R}(1, 2)\T = \tfrac{1}{5}(5, 10)\T = (1, 2)\T$ and $\M{R}(-2, 1)\T = \tfrac{1}{5}(10, -5)\T = (2, -1)\T$. ✓ The trace is $0 = 1 + (-1)$ and the determinant is $\tfrac{1}{25}(-9 - 16) = -1 = 1 \times (-1)$. ✓

Reflecting twice puts every point back, so $\M{R}^2 = \M{I}$ (in the eigenvector basis, both eigenvalues square to 1). Then $\M{R}^{25} = (\M{R}^2)^{12}\M{R} = \M{R}$.
